Principal and Accessory Muscles of Inspiration The inspiratory muscles are categorized into two groups: principal muscles and accessory muscles. The principal muscles are active during all levels of breathing, while the accessory muscles are recruited only during forced breathing, such as during intense physical activity or in certain respiratory conditions like asthma. The principal muscles of inspiration include the external intercostal muscles, the interchondral portion of the internal intercostal muscles, and the diaphragm. The external intercostal muscles and the interchondral portion of the internal intercostals function to elevate the ribs, thereby increasing the width of the thoracic cavity. The diaphragm, on the other hand, contracts to expand the vertical dimensions of the thoracic cavity and also assists in elevating the lower ribs. The accessory muscles of inspiration include the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which elevates the sternum, and the scalene muscles (anterior, middle, and posterior), which elevate the upper ribs. After intense physical exertion, individuals often adopt a posture with their hands fixed on a surface, such as a table or their knees. This posture stabilizes the insertion points of the accessory muscles, allowing their contraction to pull the origin (the upper ribs and/or sternum) and thereby assist in respiration. Muscles of Expiration During quiet breathing, expiration occurs passively due to the elastic recoil of the lungs and the rib cage, requiring minimal or no active muscle contraction. However, during active or forced breathing, specific muscles are engaged to facilitate expiration. These include the internal intercostal muscles (excluding the interchondral portion) and the abdominal muscles, such as the rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis. These muscles work to compress the thoracic cavity and force air out of the lungs. The Intercostal Muscles The intercostal muscles, along with the diaphragm, are among the most essential groups of respiratory muscles. These muscles are located between the ribs and are crucial for altering the width of the thoracic cage. There are three layers of intercostal muscles: external intercostals, internal intercostals, and innermost intercostals. The external intercostal muscles have fibers that run in an antero-inferior direction, meaning they slope forward and downward. These fibers are often referred to as front pocket muscles because their orientation resembles the direction a hand would take when placed in a front pocket. When these muscles contract, they lift the ribs, aiding in inspiration. Anteriorly, the external intercostal muscles do not attach directly to the sternum but are instead replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane. The internal intercostal muscles have fibers that run in a postero-superior direction, sloping backward and upward. These fibers are sometimes called back pocket muscles because their orientation mimics the direction a hand would take when placed in a back pocket. The internal intercostals assist in forced expiration by pulling the ribs downward and inward. Posteriorly, the internal intercostal muscles are replaced by the posterior intercostal membrane. The innermost intercostal muscles form the deepest layer and consist of three distinct parts: the subcostal muscles (located posteriorly), the innermost intercostal muscles proper (located laterally), and the transversus thoracis muscles (located anteriorly). Like the internal intercostals, the innermost intercostal muscles are also back pocket muscles and contribute to forced expiration by reducing the dimensions of the thoracic cavity.
